original_title: Resident Evil leaves the door open for more traditional, game-centric sequels
summary_en: Director Zach Cregger's new take on the survival horror franchise intentionally sidesteps the established lore, creating a narrative space for more traditional, game-faithful sequels. The film's ambiguous conclusion leaves the door wide open for future installments that could directly adapt beloved game entries.

en.title: Resident Evil Reboot's Open Ending Hints at Game-Centric Sequels
en.summary: Director Zach Cregger's new take on the survival horror franchise intentionally sidesteps the established lore, creating a narrative space for more traditional, game-faithful sequels. The film's ambiguous conclusion leaves the door wide open for future installments that could directly adapt beloved game entries.
en.body:
The latest cinematic journey into the world of **Resident Evil** has arrived, and director **Zach Cregger** has made it abundantly clear that his vision is a departure from the sprawling, lore-heavy sagas of the past. Instead of rehashing the **Spencer family** drama or the familiar reunion of **Chris and Claire Redfield**, Cregger opted for a story that runs parallel to the iconic **Resident Evil 2** and **Resident Evil 3** games. This approach, while initially met with some fan apprehension, has cleverly left the door ajar for sequels that could embrace the *exact* kind of traditional, game-centric narratives that have defined the franchise for decades.

Cregger's stated intention from the outset was to craft a film that felt *authentic to the experience* of playing the games, rather than being strictly obedient to their established canon. He succeeded by focusing on a narrative periphery, following medical courier **Bryan** (Austin Abrams) through the early days of the Raccoon City outbreak. This grounded perspective, a far cry from the super-soldiers of the games or **Milla Jovovich's** formidable Alice, allows the film to serve as a companion piece that can logically lead into more direct adaptations of game events. The film’s conclusion doesn't neatly tie everything up; instead, it plunges viewers into a moment of undeniable calamity, suggesting that containment is no longer an option and the outbreak has truly begun its relentless spread.

## A New Path for Raccoon City

This strategic narrative choice is a breath of fresh air for fans who have long clamored for cinematic adaptations that capture the essence of the games. While the **Paul W.S. Anderson** films offered action-packed spectacles, Cregger’s **Resident Evil** is positioning itself as a potential bridge to future projects that might explore the events of **Resident Evil 2** and **Resident Evil 3** with greater fidelity. The film’s success in carving out its own space within the **Resident Evil** universe means that the established lore, including the infamous **Albert Wesker** and the **S.T.A.R.S.** team, could still be integrated into future installments, perhaps in ways that feel more organic to a game-centric narrative. The film is not just an ending, but a carefully constructed beginning for a new era of **Resident Evil** cinema.

## The Future of Survival Horror on Screen

For the passionate **Resident Evil** fanbase, this open-ended approach is a cause for excitement. It signals that the franchise is willing to experiment while still respecting its roots. The ambiguity of the film's ending means that future installments can directly tackle the beloved storylines and characters from the video games, potentially offering definitive cinematic interpretations. The success of this reboot could pave the way for a slate of films that explore different eras and events within the **Resident Evil** timeline, satisfying both newcomers and long-time players. It’s a gamble that could pay off handsomely if **Cregger** and his team continue to balance originality with fan-service.

## What's Next

Details regarding potential sequels and their specific narrative focus have not yet been announced, but the groundwork has been firmly laid for **Resident Evil** to explore more traditional, game-centric storylines in the future.

content_raw: Spoiler Space  offers thoughts on, and a place to discuss, the plot points we can’t disclose in our   official review .  Fair warning: This article features plot details of Resident Evil . From the first announcement of Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil reboot, he’s been adamant that his film will not be “obedient to the lore of the games” and instead will “tell a story that feels authentic to the experience” of playing them. As Cregger spent the final weeks leading up to release pleading with gamers to give the film a chance, those same fans missed the second part of his intent: To tell a story on the periphery of the games. He succeeded, delivering a film that not only serves as a sideways companion to the first three Resident Evil games, but one that could also serve as a prequel to a more traditional take on the franchise. Gone is the sprawling sci-fi soap opera of the Spencer family, of Albert Wesker, and of Chris and Claire Redfield’s reunion. But that doesn’t mean these couldn’t eventually happen. While it might be game over for Bryan at the end of the movie, Resident Evil leaves things at the moment of open-door calamity, when containing the outbreak becomes impossible. For his version of Resident Evil , Cregger follows medical courier Bryan (Austin Abrams), a self-described glorified Postmates driver who sucks at guns—the kind of underappreciated worker who might’ve been labeled “essential” during the first days of the COVID pandemic. He’s a far cry from the S.T.A.R.S. of the game or the superheroic Alice (Milla Jovovich) from Paul W.S. Anderson’s Ozzfest-infused take on the series, though plenty of elements from Resident Evil ‘s games pop up throughout the new film.  There’s First Aid Spray in the barn, a typewriter in an office, and a distinct lack of bullets that will surely trigger some gamer PTSD. Structured like most Resident Evil games, the film moves from mundane horror settings through subterranean layers before landing in a pristine white lab, where keycard fetch quests and mixing the right chemicals are paramount. There’s even the inevitable exposition dump, which comes halfway through, when Umbrella Corporation scientist Paul (Paul Walter Hauser) and special-ops soldier Maxine (Kali Reis) pick Bryan up and give him a ride downtown. These two characters tell non-players everything they need to know about the gist of Resident Evil ‘s plot: An evil corporation lost control of a virus, and now they need guys with guns to clean it all up.  The difference is that Bryan isn’t a typical Resident Evil hero. He’s one who (kind of) survives the night by sheer luck, bolstered by his determination to get a signature for the Umbrella Corporation’s antidote he’s carrying over his shoulder.
